headline: Horsing around with the Vernon & District Drag Hounds
PostgreSQL 19's pg_plan_advice turned a 28ms query into 264ms under load
snippet: A ten-client pgbench run against a plain indexed lookup averaged 28ms a query. The same run, with one SET command telling PostgreSQL to use a sequential scan instead of the index it already wanted, averaged 264ms. Nothing else changed: same table, same data, same hardware, same query. That SET command is PostgreSQL 19's new pg_plan_advice, a contrib module that lets you hand the planner a hint string and watch it comply, or tell you exactly why it didn't. PostgreSQL 19 is still at RC2 as I write this, pulled from Docker Hub as postgres:19rc2 on 14 November. It isn't GA yet, so anything here could still shift before release. I went looking for a case where the hint would help. I didn't find one. What I found instead was a precise, well-documented way to make a healthy query slow, and a feedback system that is more honest about its own limits than most planner-hint tools I've used in other databases. The setup I built two tables: 50,000 customers and 2,000,000 orders, with status skewed so that 0.5% of orders are 'refunded' and the rest are 'shipped'. An index on status makes the refunded lookup cheap. This is the kind of table every production database has one of. CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders (status); ANALYZE; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT c.region, count(*), sum(o.amount) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'refunded' GROUP BY c.region; The planner picked an index scan on orders feeding a hash join against a sequential scan of the small customers table. Three repeated runs: 24.8ms (cold), 16.5ms, 18.0ms. That's the baseline for everything below. pg_plan_advice works in two halves. EXPLAIN (PLAN_ADVICE) tells you the advice string that would reproduce the plan you just got: Generated Plan Advice: JOIN_ORDER(o c) HASH_JOIN(c) SEQ_SCAN(c) INDEX_SCAN(o public.idx_orders_status) NO_GATHER(o c) And SET pg_plan_advice.advice = '...' feeds a string back in, which the planner then tries to honour, with feedback on how well it managed. Forcing the wrong plan I took the advice vocabulary (SEQ_SCAN, INDEX_SCAN, HASH_JOIN, NESTED_LOOP_PLAIN, and a dozen others for merge joins, partitionwise plans, and parallel workers) and used it to force the one plan the planner had already rejected: a sequential scan on orders instead of the index scan. Setup Single run Median of 3 Planner's own choice (index scan + hash join) 16.5 / 18.0 / 24.8 ms 18.0 ms Forced SEQ_SCAN(o), join left alone 46.1 / 51.7 / 43.6 ms 46.1 ms Forced SEQ_SCAN(o) + NESTED_LOOP_PLAIN(o c) 48.9 / 52.9 / 41.3 ms 48.9 ms Forcing just the scan method cost roughly as much as forcing the scan method and the join method together. The scan choice was doing almost all the work; the join strategy barely mattered once the input was a full table instead of 10,000 rows out of an index. Under concurrency the gap widened a lot further. I ran both plans through pgbench with 10 clients for 10 seconds: Plan Transactions Avg latency tps Planner's own choice 3,519 28.5 ms 351.3 Forced SEQ_SCAN(o) 384 264.0 ms 37.9 A 2.6x penalty on one connection became a 9.3x penalty on ten. Ten sequential scans over a 2-million-row table compete for the same buffer pages and CPU far harder than ten index probes do; the single-client number understates what a bad hint costs you in production. The opposite reading: I never found a case where it helped This is the part that mattered most to me. I expected to spend most of my time hunting for a query where PostgreSQL's planner gets it wrong and the hint fixes it. I built a schema where region and tier are perfectly correlated (both derived from the same id % 3), which should make the planner underestimate a combined filter on both columns under the independence assumption it still uses for most predicates. It did underestimate: a filter I knew matched 16,666 rows was costed as if it would match roughly a third of that. But the plan it picked anyway — a hash join — stayed the fastest option regardless, because the table was small enough that the misestimate never changed which plan was cheapest. I could not get PostgreSQL 19 RC2 to pick a genuinely bad default plan on this schema no matter how I skewed the correlation. Every advice string I supplied either matched what the planner already intended, or made things worse. That matches what I'd read going in: this is advice for pinning a plan you already trust, under a connection pooler or a parameter that occasionally throws the planner off, not a tool for correcting bad row estimates on the fly. I just hadn't believed it until I'd tried to break it for an hour and failed. What it refuses Three cases, with the exact feedback PostgreSQL gives: A nonexistent index: Supplied Plan Advice: INDEX_SCAN(o no_such_index) /* matched, inapplicable, failed */ Contradictory advice on the same table: SEQ_SCAN(o) /* matched, conflicting, failed */ INDEX_SCAN(o idx_orders_status) /* matched, conflicting, failed */ Both of these are refused safely — the query ran on the planner's own chosen plan, not a broken one. The one that worried me was a misspelled or missing table alias: SEQ_SCAN(zzz) /* not matched */ No error. No warning. The query just ran as if you'd supplied no advice at all, which is exactly what you'd want if you're testing, and exactly what you don't want if you've just typo'd an alias in a connection pooler's startup script and are now silently not getting the plan you think you configured. There is a documented fix: pg_plan_advice.feedback_warnings. With it on, the same typo produces a real log line: WARNING: supplied plan advice was not enforced DETAIL: advice SEQ_SCAN(zzz) feedback is "not matched" I turned it on and it did exactly what the documentation says. It's off by default, which means the failure mode most likely to bite someone — advice silently doing nothing — is also the one you have to opt into being told about. The documented caveat, and one it doesn't mention The docs warn that a cached prepared-statement plan won't notice a new pg_plan_advice.advice value until you run DISCARD PLANS. I reproduced this exactly. I forced plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan so the first EXECUTE would cache a plan, set the advice to request a sequential scan, executed once (got the seq scan, as asked), then changed the advice to request the index scan and executed again: -- exec 2, advice changed to INDEX_SCAN, plan still cached from before Finalize Aggregate -> Gather -> Partial Aggregate -> Parallel Seq Scan on orders Still the seq scan. Only after DISCARD PLANS did the next execution switch to the index scan. What the docs don't mention: EXPLAIN (PLAN_ADVICE) against that stale cached execution showed no Supplied Plan Advice section at all, because no replanning happened. If you're checking whether your new advice took effect by looking for that section, its absence looks identical to "nothing was supplied," not "your advice was ignored." I'd have assumed I'd made a typo before I'd have suspected caching. What it costs when idle With the module loaded fresh via LOAD on every transaction, a trivial single-row count ran at 0.457ms average latency against 0.408ms with the module absent entirely — a real but small 12% tax, and it's the tax of calling LOAD every time, not the module's planning hook. Preloaded once via shared_preload_libraries, the same query ran at 0.377ms, indistinguishable from not having the module at all. If you're going to use this in production, preload it; don't LOAD it per connection. What I got wrong on the way I spent close to half my testing time chasing a theory that turned out false: that a prepared statement with a parameter on the skewed status column would flip to a bad generic plan after Postgres's usual five-execution custom-plan threshold, because I assumed the generic plan would use a naive uniform-selectivity estimate for an unbound parameter. It didn't. PostgreSQL's planner already uses the column's most-common-value statistics when building the generic plan, so it picked the index scan on execution six exactly as it had on execution one — 9.99ms down to 3.3ms, with no flip at all. The "advice fixes a plan regression" post I'd half-planned to write wasn't there. The honest finding was that the planner didn't need fixing, and the correlated-columns schema in the section above was my second attempt at the same thing, which also failed to produce a bad default plan. Run it yourself This needs Docker and about ten minutes. docker run -d --name pg19 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=test postgres:19rc2 sleep 6 cat > runit.sql <<'SQL' CREATE TABLE customers (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, region text, tier text); CREATE TABLE orders (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, customer_id bigint REFERENCES customers(id), status text NOT NULL, amount numeric NOT NULL); INSERT INTO customers SELECT g, (ARRAY['eu','us','apac'])[1+g%3], (ARRAY['gold','silver','bronze'])[1+g%3] FROM generate_series(1,50000) g; INSERT INTO orders SELECT g, 1+(g%50000), CASE WHEN g % 200 = 0 THEN 'refunded' ELSE 'shipped' END, (random()*500)::numeric(10,2) FROM generate_series(1,2000000) g; LOAD 'pg_plan_advice'; -- the planner's own choice SELECT c.region, count(*), sum(o.amount) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'refunded' GROUP BY c.region; -- force a sequential scan instead SET pg_plan_advice.advice = 'SEQ_SCAN(o)'; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF, PLAN_ADVICE) SQL docker cp runit.sql pg19:/tmp/runit.sql docker exec pg19 psql -U postgres -f /tmp/runit.sql For the concurrency numbers, swap the last EXPLAIN block for a pgbench custom script with the same SET line in it and run pgbench -U postgres -n -c 10 -T 10 -f script.sql postgres against both the advised and un-advised versions. Run your own forced-scan test through pgbench with at least ten clients before you pin a plan anywhere permanent, such as a pooler's startup script or postgresql.conf. My single-connection number was 2.6x. My ten-client number was 9.3x. Production traffic looks like the second number, not the first, and I almost stopped testing before I found that out.

headline: Tru-Juice seek fifth straight win against Racing United
snippet: KINGSTON, Jamaica—Leaders Tru-Juice FC and third place Racing United will meet today in what is expected to be an exciting Legend Jamaica Premier League first round game at Ferdie Neita Park at 3:00pm. Three points separate two of the highest-scoring teams in the league whose top scorers combine for almost 25 goals and the expectations are for a high intensity game. Also today, fourth-placed Montego Bay United travels to the Edward Seaga Complex to face Tivoli Gardens; Arnett Gardens are away to last-placed Humble Lion at Effortville; Cavalier FC hosts Treasure Beach at Turner’s Oval; and Dunbeholden FC are at home to Chapelton Maroons. At Ferdie Neita Park, Tru-Juice are the inform team in the competition and will be going after a fifth straight win, coming off a win over defending champions Portmore United. As proficient as they have been scoring goals, Tru-Juice have been better at stopping goals, and have conceded just two goals in their five-game unbeaten run. Tyrone Mullings who will face the team he represented up to last season, leads the goal scoring race with eight goals so far and will spearhead the Tru-Juice attack along with Daniel Roberts, the pair having combined for 12 of the team’s 18 goals scored so far. Racing United have failed to win any of their last two games, being ambushed by Treasure Beach and were held 0-0 by Chapelton Maroons last week and will hope to rebound today. Montego Bay United have cooled after a fast start and are winless in their last four games, playing to 2-2 draws in three of them while leading on each occasion. Last weekend’s draw against Molynes United frustrated coach Javier Ainstein as they gave up two goals in the first 10 minutes, rallied to level the scores by half time, but failed to get the winner despite dominating the second half. Tivoli Gardens are also going through a poor run as well, winning just once in their last five games and have slipped to eighth place but only a point off the top six places. One positive for MBU is that top scorer Jourdaine Fletcher has scored in back to back games and has taken his tally to five so far. Both teams have been leaking at the back however and have been conceding goals. Meanwhile, Arnett Gardens are quietly moving up the ladder and are coming off a good win over Waterhouse FC after holding Mount Pleasant FA to a 1-1 draw. They are expected to get the better of Humble Lion who are at the foot of the table. Humble Lion have conceded 12 goals in four straight losses and Arnett Gardens’ Giovanni Taylor who has scored seven goals so far, will be eager to face them. Cavalier FC completed a 3-0 win over Humble Lion on Thursday, scoring twice in the remaining 15 minutes of the game that was called off on Sunday due to heavy rain. They will face a Treasure Beach team that have been inconsistent, beating Racing United, losing to Portmore, then giving up a last minute goal to draw against Dunbeholden. Cavalier are off to yet another slow start this season, as they did last term and will be looking for a run of wins to get back into the top six. A win for Dunbeholden will take them past Chapelton Maroons in the points table, on goal-difference. Chapelton will need to find a replacement for goalkeeper Prince Daniel Smith who was sent off in time added in their 0-0 draw against Racing United on Monday. headline: Abu Dhabi court orders patient to pay hospital Dh12,908 plus interest for unpaid treatment
snippet: Abu Dhabi: The Abu Dhabi Commercial Court of First Instance has ordered a patient to pay a hospital Dh12,908 for medical and treatment services he received but did not pay for, plus annual interest of 5 per cent. The hospital filed a lawsuit seeking payment of Dh12,908, along with annual legal interest of 12 per cent from the date the case was filed. It also sought court fees, expenses and lawyers’ fees. The hospital said the patient had received medical and treatment services and had failed to pay the outstanding amount. In support of its claim, the hospital submitted the patient’s medical report, a signed consent form covering admission, treatment and responsibility for the costs, and a tax invoice for the services provided. In its ruling, the court said the signed consent form confirmed that the patient had agreed to be admitted to the hospital, receive treatment and bear the cost of the medical services. The court found that this established a contractual relationship between the two parties and the basis for the patient’s obligation to pay. The tax invoice showed that Dh12,908 was due from the patient, matching the amount sought by the hospital. The court said the invoice was consistent with the medical report confirming the patient’s admission and treatment, as well as the signed consent form in which he accepted responsibility for the costs. There was no evidence that the patient had paid the outstanding balance, either in full or in part, or that his obligation to pay had ended for any other reason. The court also said the patient had not appeared to present evidence challenging the validity of the documents or proving that he had paid the debt. It therefore ordered him to pay the hospital Dh12,908, plus annual interest of 5 per cent from the date the lawsuit was filed until full payment, provided the interest does not exceed the principal debt. The patient was also ordered to pay court expenses and Dh200 in lawyers’ fees. The court rejected the hospital’s remaining claims.

headline: How to Write a Resume with ChatGPT (Step by Step)
snippet: I still remember my first resume. It was one messy page, full of long sentences, and I had no idea what a hiring manager actually wanted to see. I sent it to about twenty jobs and heard back from none of them. Years later, I understand the problem. A good resume is not a list of everything you have ever done. It is a short, clear case — made in about six seconds — that you are the right person for this one job. ChatGPT can help you build that case, if you use it the right way. Not by inventing your career, but by helping you describe what you have actually done, more clearly and more confidently. Here is the step-by-step process I use now, and the one I share with friends who are applying for a first job, changing careers, or updating a resume they wrote years ago. Before you start: gather your real details ChatGPT cannot write a good resume from nothing. It needs your real information first. Before you open it, write down: The job you want, and the job description if you have it Your work history: job titles, companies, dates, and what you actually did day to day Your education, skills, and any certificates Two or three achievements you are proud of, with numbers if you can — for example, "helped 30 new students" or "cut waiting time by 20%" Do not worry about making this neat. Just get it all in one place first. Messy notes are fine; that is what the next steps are for. Step 1: Pick a simple, clean format Recruiters in the US, UK, and Canada expect a simple layout. Skip fancy designs, colours, and photos. Most companies use an Applicant Tracking System (ATS) to scan resumes first, and unusual designs often confuse it. Use this structure: Your name and contact details A short professional summary (2–3 lines) Work experience Education Skills One page is enough if you have less than ten years of experience. Two pages is the maximum for most people. Ask ChatGPT: "What is the best simple resume format for a [your job title] in the USA? Show me the sections in order." Use its answer as your skeleton, then fill it in with your own details. Step 2: Write a professional summary that sounds like you This is the first thing a hiring manager reads, so it matters more than most people think. A weak summary sounds like this: "Hardworking and motivated individual seeking a challenging position." A good one sounds like a real person: "Customer service assistant with 3 years of experience helping busy retail customers. Good at solving problems calmly, learning new systems quickly, and working as part of a team." Try this prompt: "Write a 2–3 line professional summary for a [your job title] with [X years] of experience in [your field]. Keep it simple, honest, and specific. Do not use clichés like 'hardworking' or 'passionate'." Read what it gives you. If it sounds too generic, say: "Make it more specific to my experience in [your last job]." Keep editing until it sounds like something you would actually say about yourself. Step 3: Turn duties into achievements This is where most resumes fail. People write what they did, not what they achieved. Compare these two lines: "Responsible for handling customer complaints." "Resolved 20+ customer complaints per week, with 95% of customers leaving satisfied." The second one is stronger because it shows a result. Go through each job, one by one, and ask ChatGPT: "Here is what I did in my last job: [paste your rough notes]. Turn these into 3–4 short bullet points that show achievements, not just duties. Start each bullet with a strong action verb, and add numbers where possible. Keep each bullet to one line." Then check every bullet carefully. If ChatGPT added a number or a claim you cannot prove, remove it or change it. Never lie on a resume — it is not worth the risk, and it will catch up with you in an interview. Step 4: Match your resume to the job description This step takes about ten extra minutes, and it makes a huge difference. Copy the job description into ChatGPT and ask: "Here is a job description: [paste it]. Here is my resume so far: [paste it]. What skills and keywords from the job description am I missing? Suggest how I can add them honestly, based only on my real experience." ChatGPT will spot keywords like "teamwork", "data entry", "customer support", or "Microsoft Excel" that the ATS is looking for. Add the ones that are true for you, in your own words. Do not copy the whole job description into your resume. Step 5: Fix the wording and grammar Now paste your full resume into ChatGPT and ask: "Check this resume for grammar, spelling, and clarity. Make the language simple and professional. Do not change my facts, job titles, or dates. Tell me what you changed and why." Read the changes and keep the ones that make your resume clearer. Then read the whole resume out loud, slowly. If a sentence sounds strange when you say it, rewrite it. Your ears catch problems your eyes miss. Step 6: Make it ATS-friendly Before you send your resume anywhere, run through this quick checklist: Use a standard font like Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman Use normal headings: Work Experience, Education, Skills Save it as a PDF, unless the job asks for Word Do not use tables, text boxes, images, or fancy icons Do not include a photo, unless the job is in a country where that is normal — in the US, UK, and Canada, you do not need one Ask ChatGPT: "Check if this resume is ATS-friendly. List any formatting problems." Fix anything it flags, then save your final version with a clear file name, like Sarah-Jones-Resume.pdf. Prompts you can copy and paste Format: "What is the best simple resume format for a [job title] in the USA? Show me the sections in order." Summary: "Write a 2–3 line professional summary for a [job title] with [X years] of experience. Keep it simple and specific." Bullets: "Turn these job duties into 3–4 achievement bullet points. Start each with a strong action verb." Matching a job: "What skills and keywords from this job description am I missing from my resume?" Editing: "Check this resume for grammar and clarity. Do not change my facts, job titles, or dates." Mistakes to avoid Letting ChatGPT invent experience. If you have never used a tool, do not list it. Using the same resume for every job. Change the summary and the top bullet points for each role. Making it too long. If it is more than two pages, cut it. Forgetting to proofread. Read it once on screen, once printed, and once out loud. Then ask a friend to read it too. Final thoughts ChatGPT will not get you a job on its own. What it will do is help you explain your real experience more clearly, in less time, and with less stress. Write the first draft yourself, even if it is messy. Use ChatGPT to improve it, not to replace you. Then check every word — because at the end of the day, your name is at the top, not ChatGPT's. If you would like the full version of this guide, with more detail on each step, you can read it here: How to Write a Resume with ChatGPT (Step by Step) on TechAI Guide I also keep a collection of handy free resources on the TechAI Guide Free Tools page — worth a look while you are getting your job search organised. Good luck with your application. Take your time, be honest, and let your real experience speak for itself. What part of resume writing do you find hardest? Let me know in the comments.

headline: Why Your Stop Loss Hits, but Your Take Profit Doesn't
snippet: Have you ever been stopped out, only to watch the market reverse and move straight toward your Take Profit? You predicted the right direction, yet still lost money. Why? Sometimes, the problem isn't your analysis. It's how you choose your entry and manage your trades. 1. You're Entering Too Early Just because price reaches support doesn't mean it will immediately bounce. The market may continue falling, sweep liquidity, and only then reverse. The lesson: Wait for confirmation instead of trying to catch the exact top or bottom. 2. Your Stop Loss Is Too Tight, Your Take Profit Too Far Many traders use tight Stop Losses while targeting an ambitious 1:5 Risk-to-Reward Ratio. If your stop doesn't account for normal market volatility, your position may close before the expected move begins. The lesson: Set your Stop Loss based on market structure and your Take Profit at technically realistic levels. 3. You're Ignoring Market Liquidity Previous highs and lows often attract clusters of stop orders. Price may briefly break these levels, trigger stops, and quickly reverse. This is known as a Liquidity Sweep, although not every breakout is a liquidity grab. The lesson: Understanding liquidity helps you make better decisions about entries and stop placement. 4. You're Letting Emotions Control Your Exits Many traders widen their Stop Loss when losing but close winning trades too early. The result? Large losses and small profits, even when their market analysis is correct. The lesson: Define your risk and targets before entering, then stick to your trading plan. 🎯 Final Thoughts Getting stopped out doesn't necessarily mean your analysis was wrong. But predicting the right direction doesn't guarantee a profitable trade. A good trade requires the right combination of timing, risk management, and realistic targets. In trading, getting the direction right is only the beginning. How you manage the trade determines your long-term results. Have you ever been stopped out just before price reached your Take Profit?

headline: KHDA launches Dubai’s student protection framework for private schools: Three risk levels and a protection team in every school
snippet: Dubai: The Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA) in Dubai has launched a unified framework for student safety and protection in private education institutions, which defines the responsibilities of institutions and mechanisms for prevention, reporting and response. It also classifies cases that threaten student safety into three levels according to their degree of severity, while specifying procedures for dealing with each level. The framework includes schools, early childhood centres, higher education institutions, and vocational training and education institutes licensed by the KHDA, and covers in-person and virtual learning environments. The KHDA announced the framework during a press conference held yesterday, in the presence of the Executive Director of the Policy, Research and Programs Sector at the authority, Dr. Saeed Mubarak bin Kharbash, and the Director of the Early Childhood and Development Policies and Programs Department, Fatima Mohammed Al Janahi. Bin Kharbash stated that the well-being, quality of life, and development of learners are fundamental pillars for building the future of society. He emphasised that the framework places children and families at the heart of the social development process and clarifies the roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms for educational institutions. He added that the framework is based on the principles established by the Child Rights Law (Wadeema) and complements existing legislation and policies in the UAE and Dubai. It also supports the objectives of Dubai Social Agenda 33 and the Dubai Education Strategy 2033. He pointed out that protecting students requires effective leadership, qualified staff, and proactive parents, in addition to establishing an institutional culture that listens to students and provides them with support. Fatima Mohammed Al Janahi said that the framework defines the roles within educational institutions and obliges each school to form a student protection team, which includes the school principal as a supervisor, and at least two student protection officers who assume clear responsibilities in this area. She explained that student protection officers are responsible for monitoring cases, receiving and evaluating reports, and coordinating with specialists and senior management to determine the appropriate action, while the school principal is responsible for supervising the protection system and ensuring the effectiveness of its systems, without directly managing the cases. She added that the responsibilities include educational and academic staff and boards of trustees, in order to ensure the integration of roles and a swift response to concerns related to student safety. She indicated that the authority will work on preparing specialised training programs for those tasked with protecting students, in addition to qualifying the rest of the staff and members of the boards of trustees to deal with cases, and follow reporting and coordination procedures. Dr. Samia Al Dhaoui, an educational expert at the authority, said that the framework classifies cases that threaten the safety of students into three levels, and specifies for each the mechanisms of intervention and the parties concerned with dealing with them. She explained that high-risk cases require immediate intervention and referral to the competent authorities, including Dubai Police and ambulance services, depending on the nature of the case. As for moderately serious cases, they require intervention and follow-up according to the assessment of the protection team, with the possibility of referring them to the Community Development Authority, or coordinating with the police and ambulance when needed, and informing the KHDA to ensure coordination with parents and relevant authorities. She added that low-risk cases include initial indicators and observations monitored by the teaching staff, which do not pose a significant risk when detected, but require treatment to prevent their escalation. The institution handles them internally, while informing the authority within 72 hours. Al Dhaoui stressed that the classification gives priority to intervention for the most serious cases and helps protection teams to choose the appropriate action, noting the importance of continuous training and studying practical scenarios to raise the efficiency of these teams. The framework is based on four pillars: student protection principles, empowerment, protection procedures, and strict application of standards. It requires institutions to establish clear governance and accountability structures and define oversight and implementation roles within the protection system, ensuring clear responsibilities and effective responses. It also mandates training for staff before they begin their duties, subjecting them to regular training, and verifying their suitability to work with students. Requirements include safe recruitment procedures and additional training for staff involved in transportation, on-campus accommodation, off-campus activities and services, and digital learning environments. The scope of prevention extends to students' quality of life, promoting their participation and listening to their opinions, combating bullying, ensuring digital safety, monitoring attendance and absence, school trips and transportation, and services provided by third parties. The framework also requires institutions to provide safe channels that allow students to express and report their concerns. The framework sets pathways for reporting and escalating cases, and obliges institutions to refer any case involving a direct risk to the safety of the learner to the competent authorities without delay, as well as documenting cases, decisions and procedures, and following up on them until they are closed in accordance with the approved procedures. Institutions review their protection data at least once a semester and conduct a comprehensive annual review of their systems, while the authority monitors compliance with requirements through its oversight and regulatory procedures. A specialised team within the KHDA also follows up on child protection cases and conflict resolution, in coordination with relevant institutions and entities. The authority developed the framework in collaboration with government entities and partners in the education community, in support of Dubai’s child protection system, ‘Our Children Are a Trust’. It also published a guide for families titled ‘Together to Keep Our Children Safe and Protected’, and launched digital resources and tools to support institutions in implementing the requirements and raising awareness among staff, students, and parents. Details of the framework and supporting materials are available on its website.
